title: Nepal Expands Open-Source Electronic Medical Records Across Nineteen Public Hospitals - Bioengineer.org
description: Nepal Expands Open-Source Electronic Medical Records Across Nineteen Public Hospitals  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Nineteen government hospitals across six of Nepal’s seven provinces have transitioned to functional open-source electronic medical records, establishing integrated digital systems across multiple clinical departments. According to a community case study published in Frontiers in Digital Health, the phased deployments replaced paper records with longitudinal patient files accessible across departments, integrated laboratory and radiology results, established standardized electronic reporting, and expanded routine data available for oversight.

The health systems implementation was documented by Dipendra Gautam and colleagues from the World Health Organization country office in Nepal and the Ministry of Social Development and Health of Gandaki Province. In their assessment, the authors noted that many public hospitals in low- and middle-income countries still depend on paper documentation, which fragments patient histories, duplicates diagnostic procedures, and limits routine data essential for health management and policy planning.

Nepal’s transition toward open-source digital health platforms began in the early 2010s, utilizing Bahmni, an electronic medical record platform built on OpenMRS, as a license-free and locally adaptable alternative to proprietary software. Adoption accelerated following the COVID-19 pandemic and was reinforced by Nepal’s 2022 Joint External Evaluation and COVID-19 Intra-Action Review, both of which called for transitioning away from fragmented paper-based reporting toward integrated digital architectures.

Conducted with technical assistance from the World Health Organization and financing from the Pandemic Fund, the rollout followed a standardized six-phase model emphasizing readiness assessments, clinician engagement, local customization, and sustained capacity-building. From 2024, legacy installations were upgraded to the FHIR-aligned OpenMRS 3 interface.

Across the participating hospitals, health workers reported improvements in clinical continuity and efficiency, though the study authors noted these gains were reported by users rather than formally measured through quantitative clinical evaluations.

Reflecting on transferable lessons for comparable low- and middle-income settings, the authors concluded that public hospital transitions to electronic medical records represent organizational transformations requiring human and institutional change, rather than purely technological upgrades.

The broader case study contextualizes Nepal’s national implementation within global targets for universal health coverage and health-system resilience.

title: Crisis in Nepal Tests the Viability of International Climate Finance - THE INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS REVIEW
description: Crisis in Nepal Tests the Viability of International Climate Finance  THE INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS REVIEW
publisher.title: THE INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS REVIEW
full_article:
On August 26, 2026 catastrophic flooding struck northern and central Nepal, destroying homes and critical infrastructure and leaving thousands in need of emergency assistance. Nearly two months later, the disaster became a test for the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). On October 22, 2026 the Fund’s board agreed to set aside $20 million in relief for Nepal. The decision marks a historic step toward operationalizing international climate finance, but it raises a larger question: can international climate finance deliver support at the scale and speed required by vulnerable countries in crisis?

The Nepal Disaster and Climate Risk

The most severe damage occurred in the Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts, but damage was recorded as far as 62 miles from the floods’ origin. The Government of Nepal designated 15 municipalities across six districts as crisis-affected areas, underscoring far-reaching impacts. UN situation reports documented widespread humanitarian needs, including disruption to electricity generation, damage to agricultural land, and demand for emergency water, sanitation, and hygiene support. The scale of the damage also rendered search and rescue conditions extremely difficult, and thousands remain missing.

Scientists suspect that climate change was likely a contributing factor, although it was not the sole cause of the disaster. A glacial collapse in China’s Tibet Autonomous Region triggered an avalanche flow into the Lhende River on the China-Nepal border, sending a flood wave down the Bhotekoshi/Trishuli River corridor in Nepal. A World Weather Attribution report concluded that rising temperatures likely contributed to instability in the ice and permafrost beneath the collapsed glacier. The event illustrates how warming in the Himalayan region can compound geological hazards and expose vulnerable communities to devastating risks. The connection between the disaster and climate change substantiates Nepal’s request for financial assistance from the FRLD.

The Loss and Damage Fund

Established under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the FRLD was agreed upon at the UN Climate Conference in 2022 (COP27) and operationalized the following year (COP28, 2023). Its creation followed decades of demands from developing countries—which disproportionately face intensifying climate risks—for dedicated support to address climate-related losses that mitigation and adaptation strategies alone cannot prevent. The fund’s mandate is thus to assist particularly climate-vulnerable developing countries in addressing climate-related economic and non-economic loss and damage.

The success of the FRLD, however, depends on whether it can secure funding at the scale required and deliver it quickly and effectively to meet the urgent needs arising from climate-related disasters. Nepal’s request exposes both of these challenges.

Nepal’s Request and the UN’s Decision

Five days after the floods, on August 31, Nepal formally requested $20 million for urgent financial support from the FRLD. Although $20 million is the maximum amount that can be requested under the Fund’s current architecture, it would cover only around 0.7 percent of the estimated $5 billion in reconstruction costs. This gap makes Nepal’s request a test not only for the Fund’s ability to assist the country, but more broadly for its ability to respond to emergencies outside the standard funding process.

On October 22, the board voted to allocate the requested $20 million to Nepal and to pilot a mechanism allowing Nepal to submit a proposal outside the Fund’s regular submission window. This is a significant institutional step: it is the first allocation for an immediate response to a specific climate-related disaster. However, the decision does not mean the money has been disbursed. Nepal must now submit a formal application for board approval. No firm timeline for this process has been announced, and unless it is further expedited, next steps may not occur until the next board meeting scheduled for December 2026.

The decision therefore reveals a contradiction. The Fund has shown that it can make an exceptional allocation in response to an emergency, but the remaining approval process could undermine the urgency this allocation is intended to address. Without expedited disbursement, the Fund risks providing retrospective financial assistance rather than an effective response to the immediate needs created by a climate disaster. By the time funds reach affected communities, it may be too little, too late.

Two Constraints on Meaningful Climate Finance

The Nepal disaster reveals two central constraints on the FRLD’s effectiveness. First, the Fund’s resources remain far below the scale of need. During its first operational phase in 2025, developing countries submitted 176 applications requesting a total of $2.8 billion while pledges to the fund have only reached $822 million. This financing gap raises doubts about whether an under-resourced fund can keep pace with unfolding climate emergencies without forcing vulnerable countries to compete for scarce resources. The Fund needs significantly more financial resources, and wealthier countries must provide larger, more frequent, and more predictable contributions.

Second, the Nepal case exposes the limitations of conventional funding procedures during sudden disasters. The October decision was an exceptional response, but the Fund lacks an established, rapid-access funding pathway for emergencies. Furthermore, while the October decision allocates the requested funds, it remains to be seen whether or when those funds will be disbursed. The FRLD should develop a permanent emergency mechanism to respond to climate crises like the floods in Nepal. The framework should establish clear eligibility criteria, expedited review, and transparent timelines for approving and disbursing funds. The Fund’s response to Nepal will verify whether the FRLD can meet the urgent demands of disaster recovery.

The Nepal case before the FRLD demonstrates a central tension in climate finance: although responding to climate-related loss and damage is increasingly recognized as an international responsibility, meaningful financial assistance remains difficult to deliver. The FRLD’s October 22 decision sets an important precedent, but its credibility will depend on whether Nepal receives funding promptly and whether future emergencies can count on the same support. Without greater financial resources and faster response procedures, the Fund is at risk of failing to fulfill its mandate.

title: Nepal Pledges to Implement LIAF-AR Facility for Climate Change Adaptation - Ratopati
description: Nepal Pledges to Implement LIAF-AR Facility for Climate Change Adaptation  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Turkey. Nepal has expressed its commitment to implement the 'Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience' (LIAF-AR) facility in accordance with the needs and priorities of local communities affected by climate change.

Minister of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, Gita Chaudhary, stated that Nepal considers the LIAF-AR facility, established to enhance the climate adaptation capacity of Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and advance climate action at the local level, as a significant opportunity.

Speaking at the official launch event of the LIAF-AR facility held here on Wednesday on the sidelines of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP-31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, she reiterated the government's commitment to channeling climate finance to local communities and ensuring their participation in climate planning and decision-making processes.

Minister Chaudhary emphasized the need to utilize LIAF-AR not just as a mechanism for financial assistance, but as an opportunity to bring about transformation in the planning, financial management, and implementation systems of climate action.

She informed that Nepal had already signed a Memorandum of Understanding with LIAF-AR on May 8, 2026 (Baisakh 25) and that the process for its establishment is underway. She stated that the government is committed to enhancing the capacity of local governments and institutions, empowering communities, and ensuring that citizens affected by climate finance directly benefit.

Mentioning that Nepal, despite contributing negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions, is facing severe impacts of climate change, she said that the risk of climate-induced disasters is rapidly increasing in the mountainous and hilly regions.

She presented the devastating disaster in the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi region last September as a serious example of climate risk. According to preliminary reports, she informed that more than 1,457 people died and 5,285 are still missing in the disaster. She stated that about 60,000 people from approximately 15,000 families were directly affected by the disaster.

According to the preliminary rapid assessment by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, an estimated US$4.78 billion is required for post-disaster recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction, she said. This amount is equivalent to about 10 percent of Nepal's Gross Domestic Product.

She noted that the disaster caused significant damage not only to physical infrastructure and livelihoods but also to settlements, cultural heritage, social structures, and natural resources, and stated that the economic value of some damages cannot even be determined.

Stating that disasters are recurring frequently, especially in the mountainous regions due to climate change, and their impact is becoming more severe, she said that adequate, predictable, additional, easily accessible, and grant-based climate finance is necessary for adaptation and to address loss and damage. She also stressed the need to increase investment in climate information services, early warning systems, technical capacity, and modern technology.

Mentioning that the locally-led approach of LIAF-AR is particularly important for climate-vulnerable countries like Nepal, Minister Chaudhary expressed the view that communities most affected by climate change should be empowered to lead the identification of solutions, planning, and implementation.

She thanked the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED), which serves as the secretariat for LIAF-AR, and stated that Nepal fully supports the goal of advancing this initiative under the leadership and ownership of the LDCs.

Minister Chaudhary called on the international community to expand cooperation and partnership with the LIAF-AR facility. Informing that Nepal will host the 15th Board meeting of LIAF-AR in Kathmandu next year, she invited the LDC Chair, Board members, and relevant stakeholders to visit Nepal.

Representatives from various partner organizations participated in the program.

Minister Chaudhary also informed that through various programs organized at the Nepal Pavilion established at COP-31, Nepal's mountain ecosystem, climate vulnerability, disaster experiences, climate actions, and the livelihoods of mountain communities will be presented to the international community.

She reiterated the commitment to continue collaboration with the LDC Group and LIAF-AR partners with the objective of implementing climate commitments at the local level and leaving no vulnerable community behind.

title: Nepal-Tibet floods showed the need for greater climate finance. Is the world listening? - The Conversation
description: Nepal-Tibet floods showed the need for greater climate finance. Is the world listening?  The Conversation
publisher.title: The Conversation
full_article:
Earlier this year, a massive flash flood ripped through Nepalese and Tibetan townships along the Bhote Koshi river system, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and at least 5,000 missing.

Climate change contributed to the glacial mountain collapse that triggered the floods. But Nepal, a developing country of about 30 million people, only produces 0.05% of the world’s carbon emissions.

Left with a multi-billion dollar reconstruction bill, Nepal is a clear-cut example of the need for greater climate finance – the funding to help developing countries protect their people and economies against climate disasters, and rebuild when they happen.

But time and time again, United Nations climate summits fall short of agreements that would provide enough climate finance to match the magnitude of climate change. Will COP31 be any different?

Read more: Climate disasters will send many countries into a debt spiral – but there’s a way out

The Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen, is this year’s president of negotiations. He sits with André Corrêa do Lago, who was the president of last year’s climate summit. Gokhan Balci/Getty

What is climate finance?

Climate finance is the funding that helps countries protect their people and economies from the damage wrought by global warming. It includes projects like building sea walls to protect from floods and sea-level rise, developing drought-tolerant crops or enhancing infrastructure so buildings and transport networks can withstand extreme weather. Climate finance can also fund investments that mitigate – or reduce – carbon emissions, such as renewable energy and electric transport.

Since climate diplomacy began in 1995 with the first UN climate summit, developing countries – particularly in the Pacific – have fought for greater availability of climate finance.

Their argument is this: wealthy countries should lead on climate finance because they developed with the benefit of fossil fuels, and contribute the most to climate change. In comparison, developing countries have limited resources, and emit negligible amounts of greenhouse gases but suffer disproportionate climate consequences.

At the 2024 climate summit in Baku, Azerbaijan, a new finance agreement was reached. Developed countries committed to raise US$300 billion (A$436 billion) a year for the world’s poorest nations by 2035. This might sound ambitious, but it is nowhere near enough to address the global need.

At the recent pre-COP31 talks in Fiji, Pacific leaders made it abundantly clear climate finance was crucial for the survival of vulnerable countries.

What is climate ‘loss and damage’?

Developing countries, such as those in the Himalayas as well as small island nations, are particularly vulnerable to climate change because of their geographic exposure, reliance on sectors such as agriculture and lower capacity to adapt. The concept of “loss and damage” reflects the unavoidable and irreversible harm from climate change.

The push to secure an official UN-backed loss and damage fund was a contentious and decades-long process, fraught with resistance from wealthy nations. So developing nations were jubilant at the close of COP27 in Eygpt in 2022, when wealthy countries finally agreed to establish a fund to respond to loss and damage.

This fund made its first call for submissions at COP30 in Belém in 2025, and received almost 180 requests totalling US$2.8 billion (A$4 billion) by the June 2026 deadline. While pledges to the fund now exceed US$820 million (A$1.2 billion), there is a significant financing gap compared to the demand.

What exactly this fund will pay for, and how, is unclear. However, the catastrophe on the Nepal-Tibet border served as the first litmus test. Nepal made an urgent appeal to the fund and asked for an emergency payout of the maximum allowable amount of US$20 million (A$29 million).

At its first ever extraordinary meeting, the fund’s board decided to set aside US$21.6 million (A$31 million). This is only about 0.7% of Nepal’s actual economic loss and damage cost. And it doesn’t include non-economic losses related to health, culture or nature.

The speed of that decision is historic in the notoriously snail-paced UN process. Other countries will have to wait until December 2026 for the outcome of their submissions.

Conference participants in the Moana Blue Pacific pavilion at the COP31 climate conference. Pacific nations have pushed hard for greater climate finance to be made available. Burak Kara/Getty Images

How Australia should act

As the president of COP31 negotiations, Australia’s climate minister Chris Bowen has an opportunity to elevate the topics that Turkey is strategically avoiding. These include the need for a fossil fuel phase-out – only by reducing greenhouse gas emissions can disasters such as the one in Nepal be prevented. Australia must also be an ally to island nations across the Pacific.

In terms of finance, Australia should rally more support for the Pacific Resilience Facility. This Pacific-owned and led fund acts as a self-sustaining financial model. It relied on an endowment fund structure designed to generate predictable, continuous returns, eliminating the need for repeating donation cycles or accumulating national debt. This fund aims to directly benefit communities on the ground, including addressing loss and damage. But it requires more long-term investment.

Ultimately, no amount of finance can respond to the damage that climate change is already causing across the globe. It is absolutely vital that COP31 genuinely focuses on eliminating its root cause: the human use of fossil fuels.

title: Bangladesh and Nepal Get Three More Years To Prep for Loss of U.N.'s 'Least Developed Country' Status - RANE Worldview
description: Bangladesh and Nepal Get Three More Years To Prep for Loss of U.N.'s 'Least Developed Country' Status  RANE Worldview

full_article:
(Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP via Getty Images)

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the U.N. headquarters in New York City on Sept. 24, 2026.

Bangladesh and Nepal will use the Least Developed Country graduation extension to strengthen economic resilience, with Bangladesh prioritizing export diversification, alternative trade arrangements and macroeconomic reforms, while Nepal focuses on expanding hydropower exports, attracting investment and addressing infrastructure and climate-related vulnerabilities, although the extension is more likely to provide temporary relief and improve short-term transition preparedness than deliver significant structural change. On Oct. 29, the U.N. General Assembly granted Bangladesh and Nepal a three-year extension to their LDC graduation period, postponing their exit from Nov. 24, 2026, to Nov. 24, 2029. Both countries had met the graduation criteria but requested additional time to prepare for the loss of LDC-specific support, which includes preferential access to international markets and eligibility for targeted U.N. and multilateral financing and technical assistance programs, citing the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, climate-related disasters and geopolitical disruptions.

title: Hindus across Nepal celebrate Bhai Tika; sisters pray for brothers long life - Daily Excelsior
description: Hindus across Nepal celebrate Bhai Tika; sisters pray for brothers long life  Daily Excelsior
publisher.title: Daily Excelsior
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nov 11: Hindus across Nepal on Wednesday celebrated Bhai Tika, the final day of the five-day Deepawali festival, with sisters performing rituals for their brothers and praying for their good health, prosperity and long life.

Also known as Yama Panchak, Bhai Tika is marked by sisters garlanding their brothers and applying a mixture of vermilion, rice and curd on their foreheads. They also offer them sweets, fruits and other delicacies, while brothers reciprocate with gifts or cash.

The five-day festival begins with the worship and feeding of crows, followed by dogs and cows, and the worship of Goddess Laxmi. It concludes with the celebration of the bond between brothers and sisters.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah, in his message on the occasion, said traditional festivals play an important role in bringing people together by encouraging them to set aside differences and fostering social unity, harmony and tolerance.

He said Bhai Tika strengthens the bonds of love, affection and mutual respect between brothers and sisters, thereby promoting family unity and togetherness.

Highlighting the festival's religious significance, Shah recalled the Hindu mythological legend of Yamaraj and his sister Yamuna.

According to the legend, Yamaraj visited his sister's home in Kartik following her invitation, where Yamuna welcomed him with traditional rituals and applied tika on his forehead.

Citing the popular belief associated with the tradition, Shah said Yamaraj, the god of death, blessed brothers who receive tika and worship from their sisters on this day with long life, good health and prosperity. (PTI)
